title: Trauma induced teaching isn't unique
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner builds on Pamela Snow's analysis of trauma-informed education to make a counterintuitive argument: the practices that research recommends for trauma-affected students are identical to the practices recommended by cognitive science for all students. The article presents Snow's side-by-side comparison of what trauma-affected children need and how explicit teaching informed by cognitive load theory addresses those same needs. A trauma-affected student needs a predictable, orderly environment; so does every student. They need educators to be clearly in charge of learning; so does every novice learner. They need instruction broken into manageable chunks; so does anyone trying to learn something new. Kirschner concludes that 'good instruction is good instruction'—not because trauma is irrelevant, but because the foundational conditions of effective learning (psychological safety, teacher-led instruction, minimized distractions, warm calling, gradual release of responsibility, retrieval practice) are what makes learning accessible to all students, including those with the most challenging backgrounds. The implication for school leaders and teachers is that trauma-informed practice and evidence-based instructional practice are not in tension—they converge on the same set of classroom conditions.
points: The needs of trauma-affected students and the requirements of good instructional practice converge on the same classroom conditions: predictability, educator-led instruction, minimized distractions, high expectations, and structured participation—meaning trauma-informed practice and evidence-based teaching are not competing frameworks.

Room design matters for trauma-affected and neurotypical students alike: stand-alone classrooms, rows facing the teacher for instruction, minimized visual distractions, and quiet transitions are not just trauma accommodations—they are the conditions under which all novice learners acquire new knowledge most effectively.

The gradual release of responsibility (I do, we do, you do) addresses both the trauma need for predictable adult authority and the cognitive science requirement for managing cognitive load in novice learners.

Pseudoscientific tools and practices harm trauma-affected students not because of anything specific to trauma, but because they harm all students: discovery learning, learning styles inventories, and whole language reading approaches violate the cognitive conditions necessary for learning regardless of background.

Cold calling—reframed as 'warm calling'—serves both trauma-informed and instructionally effective goals: ensuring all children participate in classroom learning, with adjustments and accommodations as needed, conveys that the teacher expects every student to learn.
quotes: What struck me is that what a student with trauma needs corresponds one-to-one with what every student needs, namely, good instruction in a psychologically safe environment. Of course, different children with different needs need more of one thing and less of another, but the principles remain the same. Good instruction is good instruction.

Learning spaces should be stand-alone classrooms, not open-plan environments with inadequate sound dampening and constant visual distraction from other classrooms. Children should be seated in rows, facing the teacher when they are being taught new knowledge and skills.
Classrooms should be calm, orderly and predictable learning spaces, as a reflection of taught behaviour expectations and adult-led limit-setting with clear, consistent and fair consequences.
Instruction should be educator-led. Educators take responsibility for the teaching of new content. This is not left to chance via discovery learning.

Device use is minimal to non-existent. Except in timetabled IT classes, technology has little to no intrinsic learning benefit in classrooms. Pseudoscientific tools and practices are not in use (e.g., Learning Styles / Multiple Intelligences Inventories; Brain Gym; Whole Language/Balanced Literacy approaches to reading instruction; discovery learning for maths).

Non-volunteers are called on (so-called 'cold-calling' – better described as 'warm calling') to respond to carefully framed questions about material that has been taught. This ensures that all children participate in classroom learning, with adjustments and accommodations if needed, to support this.
